'''''Torreya californica''''' is a species of [[conifer]] endemic to [[California]], occurring in the [[Pacific Coast Ranges]] and the foothills of the [[Sierra Nevada]]. It is commonly known as '''California torreya''' or '''California nutmeg tree'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TOCA|taxon=Torreya californica|accessdate=11 December 2015}}</ref> (although not closely related to true [[nutmeg]]). It is one of only two species of genus ''[[Torreya]]'' that are native to North America. A slow-growing (but long-lived) subcanopy tree, it is listed as "vulnerable" in the [[IUCN Red List]].<ref name="redlist" />

==Description==

California torreya is an [[evergreen]] tree growing to {{Convert|15–27|m}} tall,<ref name="tktimb">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |pages=105}}</ref> with a trunk diameter of {{Convert|0.5–1|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}, exceptionally 2 m. In full sun, the crown is conical in overall shape, with whorled branches. But in subcanopy shade, the tree may grow leaning and sometimes multi-stem.

The species has a [[taproot]]. The bark is thin, from 0.8–1.3 cm on mature trees. The leaves are needle-like, stiff, sharp-pointed, {{Convert|3-8|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long<ref name="tktimb" /> and persisting for many years. They are arranged spirally, but twisted at the base to lie flat either side of the shoots.<ref name=feis />

As with all species of ''[[Torreya]]'', the male ([[pollen]]) [[conifer cone|cones]] are 5–7 mm long, grouped in lines along the underside of a shoot. The female ([[seed]]) cones are single or grouped two to five together near the end of a short stem and require about 18 months to mature into a [[drupe]]-like structure with the single large [[nut (fruit)|nut]]-like seed 2.5–4 cm long. The seed is surrounded by a fleshy covering that becomes dark green to purple at full maturity in late autumn.<ref name=feis />

On serpentine rock, California torreya becomes a stunted tree or shrub and occurs only on north-facing slopes in coastal chaparral.<ref name="redlist">{{cite web |title=California Nutmeg, ''Torreya californica'' |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/34026/2840781#assessment-information |website=IUCN Redlist |date=27 April 2011 |access-date=16 September 2022}}</ref>

It is capable of resprouting following disturbance such as fire, although regrowth is slow.<ref name="redlist" />

== Etymology ==
''Torreya'' is named for Dr. [[John Torrey]] (1796–1873), an [[America]]n botanist who contributed to the ''[[Flora of North America]]''.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 84, 382</ref>

''Californica'' means 'from [[California]]'.<ref name="gledhill" />

==Distribution and habitat==

The altitudinal range of ''T. californica'' is from near sea level (but usually above 200 m) in the Coast Ranges to {{Convert|2,500|m|abbr=on}} in the [[Sierra Nevada]].<ref name="redlist" /> This shade-adapted, subcanopy tree is native to mountainous habitats in either the [[California Coast Ranges]] or the west slopes of the [[Cascade Range | Cascade]] and Sierra Nevada mountain ranges in California, which are distant from the coast. In the Coast Ranges, it is distributed from southwest Trinity County south to Monterey County. In the interior mountain ranges, it is distributed from Shasta County south to Tulare County.<ref name="feis">{{cite web |title=Torreya californica |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/tree/torcal/all.html |website=Fire Effects Information System (FEIS) |publisher=U.S. Forest Service |access-date=16 September 2022}}</ref>

Mountainous terrain affords this narrowly dispersed ancient [[conifer]] opportunities to track suitable [[microclimate]]s by shifting [[altitude]] and local [[topography]], along with shifts between northerly (cool) and southerly (warm) slope [[aspect (geography) | aspect]]s or deep ravines and canyons, while remaining on the same mountain. Short distance adjustments are crucial for this genus, as squirrels and humans seem to be the most active agents for seed dispersal.<ref name=Barlow2001>{{Cite magazine |last=Barlow |first=Connie |date=2001 |title=Anachronistic Fruits and the Ghosts Who Haunt Them |url=http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/618.pdf |magazine=Arnoldia |volume=61 |issue=2 |pages=19–21 |location=Boston, Massachusetts |publisher=Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University |access-date=2014-07-26 |archive-date=12 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130212155715/http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/618.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The patchiness of its geographic range is a form of [[disjunct distribution]]. The species is considered to be rare, but wherever it is found in the wild it may be locally abundant. This pattern of distribution is suggestive of a [[Relict (biology) | relict taxon]] that has had difficulties navigating episodes of [[climate change]] in which range shifts had to occur in topographically complex landscapes. A sister species in eastern North America, [[Torreya taxifolia | Florida torreya]], was reduced to only a single population owing to episodes of climate change during the [[Quaternary glaciation]]. Its status as a [[glacial relict]] was recognized in its listing as an [[endangered species]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, Final Rule to Determine Torreya taxifolia (Florida torreya) to be an Endangered Species |journal=Federal Register |date=23 January 1984 |volume=49 |issue=15 |pages=2783–2786 |url=https://ecos.fws.gov/docs/federal_register/fr789.pdf |access-date=17 July 2021}}</ref> 

Range shifts would have been difficult for all species of genus ''Torreya''. [[Rodent]]s are the only abundant and dependable seed dispersers — yet they gather and cache the large seeds only short distances.<ref name=Barlow2001/>

== Ecology ==

''Torreya'' species are all adapted to establish and grow slowly as subcanopy woody plants in forest habitats of moderate to dense shade. In this way, their leaf structure and growth habit resemble species of yew, genus ''[[Taxus]]'', which is a close relative.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cope |first1=Edward A |date=October 1998 |title=Taxaceae: The Genera and Cultivated Species |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4354329 |journal=Botanical Review |volume=64 |issue=4 |pages=291–322 |doi=10.1007/BF02857621 |jstor=4354329 |s2cid=42399351|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

''Torreya'' species are found in late seral and climax communities. Owing to their ability to resprout from the root crown after logging or mild fire, the species will experience growth opportunities in the early stages of regrowth forest habitats.<ref name="feis" />

When a tree-fall opens the forest canopy (or if nearby roadbuilding occurs), then upward growth will be stimulated.<ref name="tg-calif">{{cite web |last1=Barlow |first1=Connie |title=''Torreya californica'' (California torreya) |url=http://www.torreyaguardians.org/california.html |access-date=18 June 2022 |website=Torreya Guardians}}</ref>

Stems will lean in very shady conditions, in quest of patches of sunlight. Extremely leaning stems within a shady subcanopy gather [[moss]] as they age. An old leaning stem that fails to access sunlight will perish, but not before the long-lived [[root crown]] has given rise to one or more younger stems searching for sunlight in different directions.<ref name="tg-calif" />

Seed production occurs on female branches (and trees) only in the presence of direct sunlight. Because the ''Torreya'' genus has very long-lived roots, it can continue slow growth, while replenishing basal stems, for many decades without seed production becoming crucial for the persistence of a local population.<ref name="tg-history">{{cite web |last1=Barlow |first1=Connie |title=Natural History of ''Torreya taxifolia'' |url=http://www.torreyaguardians.org/torreya.html |access-date=20 June 2022 |website=Torreya Guardians}}</ref>

=== Threats ===
[[File:Torreya californica resprouts after wildfire.jpg|thumb|A tree resprouts after wildfire killed its main stems (yellow), but not their root crowns, in California's [[Robert Louis Stevenson State Park |Stevenson State Park]] (2019)|left|upright=1.4]]

The [[IUCN Red List]] bases its assessment of "vulnerable" in this way:

"Past logging has virtually eliminated ''Torreya californica'' from parts of its historic range and also removed most of the large trees across almost all of its range. Regrowth is reported to be very slow. On this basis a past decline of more than 50% of mature trees in the population has been inferred over the past 150 years (three generations), leading to an assessment of Vulnerable under the A1 criterion.... Logging in the late 19th and up to the mid 20th centuries virtually eliminated California Nutmeg from the Vaca Mountains of Napa and Solano counties, and considerably reduced populations in the Santa Cruz Mountains and lower Russian River area of Sonoma County (Howard 1992). Logging also eliminated many of the larger trees in the remainder of its range and resulted in a decline of mature trees in the total population, which is only now slowly being restored. As this species is dependent on forest cover, deforestation in parts of California has further contributed to a decline. On this basis it is reasonable to infer an historic decline in the number of mature trees of at least 50%. This decline has now ceased or virtually ceased."<ref name="redlist" />

The "severe fragmentation" of the population was also listed as a risk element for the species. [[Wildfire]], however, was not mentioned as one of the risks. Perhaps this is because the most recent IUCN assessment is listed as April 2011 — just before the extraordinary increase in the scale and intensity of [[list of California wildfires|California wildfires]].

== Champion trees ==
{{multiple image
| total_width       = 350
| image1            = Torreya californica 2005 champion base.jpg
| image2            = Torreya californica 2005 champion top.jpg
| footer            = In 2005, then-champion California torreya tree was already showing signs of decline in its moss-covered trunk and multi-stem top, by Scott Creek north of [[Santa Cruz, California|Santa Cruz]].
}}

Champion trees are compared by a total of three measurements: trunk circumference, height, and crown spread. Hence, when the crown seriously deteriorates, a champion can lose its status even before death.<ref name=champion>{{cite web |title=California Nutmeg |url=https://www.americanforests.org/tree/california-nutmeg-ca/ |website=AmericanForests.org |publisher=American Forests Champion Trees Official Register |access-date=22 June 2022}}</ref>

The earliest recorded "champion" torreya grew near Fort Bragg in Mendocino County. It measured 43 meters in height and 4.5 meters in diameter, but it was cut by timber thieves. Ring counts of the remnants left by the thieves yielded an age of 236 years old. However, the center was rotted out, so an estimate had to be made. The likely age (reported by Frank Callahan) was thus between 275 and 286 years.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Callahan |first1=Frank |title=Medford Oregon ex-situ locale for seed-producing Florida Torreya |url=http://www.torreyaguardians.org/oregon-ex-situ.html |website=Torreya Guardians |access-date=16 September 2022}}</ref>

As of 2005, the champion tree was along Scott Creek north of Santa Cruz. Lee Klinger (shown for scale in the photo) measured that tree's circumference: 6.4 meters. It was already showing signs of decline, including moss indicative of very slow growth on the multiple stems of its crown and on its trunk.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Barlow |first1=Connie |title=Coast Range ''Torreya californica'' in the Scotts Creek watershed |url=http://www.torreyaguardians.org/swanton.html |website=Torreya Guardians |access-date=22 June 2022}}</ref>

In 2014 a new champion was nominated and named, still in the Santa Cruz Mountains. Its trunk circumference was only 3.4 meters, but it was healthy and had a height of 32 meters and a crown spread of 18 meters.<ref name=champion />

==Uses==
{{multiple image
| total_width       = 450
| image1            = Torreya_californica_full_of_seeds_at_the_Swanton_RR_station.jpg
| caption1          = A torreya tree (thick, auburn trunk) has a huge crop of seeds from decades of full sun. Scott Creek, Santa Cruz.
| image2            = Torreya californica Scott Creek 2005 03.jpg
| caption2          = Close-up of a seed-rich branch. Scott Creek, 2005.
}}

Commercial harvesting of California nutmeg is almost nonexistent due to scant availability.  It was logged on a limited basis in the past, especially where growing in association with [[coast redwood]], but was never an important timber species.<ref name=feis />

The fine-grained, yellow-brown wood is highly durable. It is strong and elastic, smooth in texture, polishes well, and emits a fragrance similar to that of sandalwood.<ref name=feis /> The wood is sometimes used in making [[Go (game)#Boards|Go game boards]], as a cheaper substitute for the prized [[Torreya nucifera|''kaya'']] (''Torreya nucifera'') of [[Japan]] and [[Southeast Asia]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bozulich |first1=Richard |title=The Go Player's Almanac |date=1992 |publisher=Ishi Press International |isbn=9784871870405 |pages=142–155}}</ref>

The seeds were once mentioned in pharmacognostic literature under the Latin name ''nux moschata Californica''.<ref name=Wigg1855>{{cite journal|last=Wiggers|first=H. A. L.|title=Bericht über die Leistungen in der Pharmacognosle und Pharmacie|journal=Canstatt's Jber. Fortschr. Pharm.|year=1855|volume=4|issue=1|pages=1–210|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aYhbAAAAQAAJ}}</ref>

The seeds were reportedly a highly valued food of Indigenous peoples in California, though they are inedible raw.<ref name="tktimb" /> Additionally, the roots were used for making baskets and the wood for making bows.<ref name=feis /><ref>{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=Stephen |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf |location=New York |isbn=0-394-73127-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/416 416] |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/416 }}</ref>
